thesis: William Hooper bet everything — his fortune, his family, his father's love — on a principle of sovereignty, and the fact that the revolution he bankrupted himself for didn't reimburse him reveals the core mechanic of every state: the founders are just the first to be extracted from.
stakes: If you've ever poured your own resources into a cause, a business, or a movement expecting the system to reward your loyalty, Hooper's story is your warning label. The state doesn't honor its founding invoices — it collects and moves on.
counterpoint: Hooper chose his path with open eyes and could have remained a comfortable Loyalist like his father; his ruin was the cost of conscience, not betrayal by the state. But that framing lets the system off the hook — the cause didn't fail, the payment structure did.
implication: Sovereignty is a practice, not a pension plan. If you're going to fund a revolution — political, commercial, or personal — understand that the entity you're building may be the first to forget what you spent.
close: Hooper signed his name to a document that promised freedom and got his house burned for it and his bank account emptied. The estate at Finian is ash now, and so is the idea that the system will ever settle its debts with the people who built it. Fund your own revolution — and never expect a receipt.
